TRANSNET PIPELINE FUEL THEFT

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Fuel is like liquid gold on the black market – its’ hard to trace and it’s quick to sell. We investigate a brazen new crime trend targeting fuel pipelines across the country - that’s not only

Unique Selling Point:
** DRONE FOOTAGE
** NEW CRIME TREND


Summary:
Fuel in South Africa is a top commodity. Hundreds of Millions of litres is transported across the country every week. Criminals are tapping in and feeding a lucrative black market with stolen fuel. The latest crime trend is targeting Transnet’s extensive pipeline network that traverses five province. The modus operandi of the criminals suggest well-organised and equipped gangs are driving the hits. Using engineering equipment, the thieves tap into the pipeline stealing tankers and tankers full of fuel. In the past three months, Transnet had recorded over 200 incidents along its pipeline – pipeline thefts are on the rise. It’s not petty crime – this amounts to essential infrastructure damage and could see very hefty sentences in successful case prosecution.

We highlight this new crime trend while getting an inside track from one of the gangs in this Carte Blanche investigation.

Further information:
Fuel in South Africa is a top commodity. Hundreds of Millions of litres is transported across the country every week. Criminals are tapping in and feeding a lucrative black market with stolen fuel. The latest crime trend is targeting Transnet’s extensive pipeline network that traverses five province.

The modus operandi of the criminals suggest well-organised and equipped gangs are driving the hits. Using engineering equipment, the thieves tap into the pipeline stealing tankers and tankers full of fuel. In the past three months, Transnet had recorded over 200 incidents along its pipeline – pipeline thefts are on the rise. It’s not petty crime – this amounts to essential infrastructure damage and could see very hefty sentences in successful case prosecution.

South Africa's infrastructure is being damaged by this theft and vandalism along Transnet’s 3 800km fuel pipeline network. The pipeline network traverses five provinces and transports 250 million liters of petrol and diesel per week.

In the past 18 months, Transnet had recorded loses of over 16 million litres to these thefts.

The thefts occur in Gauteng and Mpumalanga mainly, however the incidents had become more sporadic along its entire network recently.

Transnet said evidence obtained about the modus operandi of the criminals pointed to a well-organised and equipped gang being involved. “Criminals operate in groups, each with a specific task. These criminals are found to be armed, [and they have] no fear for their personal safety.”

It’s believed that the criminals approached landowners and promise them financial compensation in exchange for access to land and pipelines.

We speak to an affected Farmer, look at the environmental damage, get the inside track from an informant and speak to a security company tackling this crime trend with state of the art technology and old-school intelligence.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Fuel is like liquid gold on the black market. We have exposed many methods used by criminal syndicates over the years – from diesel skimming to hijacking petrol tankers and robbing petrol depots.

LINK: Criminals now target fuel pipelines, they're buried at least two meters underground. It's more labor intensive, but the rewards are worth the effort.

ANDREA: Millions of litres of fuel are stolen at any given time, on any given week, at any given point from which the pipeline runs.

VO: This is a priority crime for the Criminal Justice System. Fuel is a crucial commodity and the pipelines are essential infrastructure, , explains Advocate Andrea Johnson from the NPA.

ANDREA: It has a ripple effect. So it doesn't just affect the economy, it will affect society. And I think in the long run, it will affect our ability to sustain ourselves in terms of the functions we need to perform using fuel.

VO: Every week, Transnet Pipelines delivers two hundred and fifty million litres of fuel - that’s the equivalent of 1000 petrol tankers on the road every day. The network of over 3800 km of pipelines covers 5 provinces.

One of these lines runs through Farm Manager JP Morkel’s operation in Mpumalanga.

He was shocked when he stumbled across this scene earlier in the year.

MASA: When you come out, is it just like overflowing and just spilling and spilling?
JP: It was basically what you call it, a borrelbad, It was almost as if you took your shovel and hit one of your water pipes in your house, that the water just starts spraying and spraying, I think, at 10 to 20 times the pressure.

VO: The thieves dug a two by two meter hole by hand in the middle of corn fields under the cover of darkness.

JP: These clearly marked tracks where they drove actually over our corn that was planted and that was already standing on the field where they just came in. There were smaller tracks, but it was definitely a link truck that you could see.

VO: In recent months, JP knows of at least three other incidents in the area - most of the farm owners had no knowledge of the pipeline’s existence.

We took to the sky to get a better understanding of the challenges in detecting this crime trend, that is largely carried out in very remote areas.

LINK: The pipes aren't visible to the naked eye, so they must be working with insiders to get information.

WAAL: they will recruit anybody, they've got the money on their side that they can throw around

VO: Waal de Waal’s private security company has investigated some of these cases. He says budgets for bribes are not an issue for these thieves.

WAAL: If you if you think of getting the fuel for 10 grand, 57 ran a truck. Forty thousand litres. That's 420000. The truck. We had instances where they came with six bowsers in one night. Imagine the money that they can play with.

VO: This is an informant. He was recruited by one of the pipeline theft syndicates. He says paying bribes to ensure successful hits was part of their modus operandi.

INFORMANT: They will say if they have money that is nothing can stop them. Depending on your position. Just one day they get 40 thousand and some of them 20, some hundreds

VO They would come in gangs of 10 to 15 people to steal - armed with tools, muscle and expertise.

INFORMANT: those bakkies have everything I have Spanel to open the valves and pipes and those guys know how to feed the pipes into the valve. M11// There are people that have experience with this thing

VO: By this stage, insiders would have pointed out the location, others would have been paid off to look the other way, so that the guys in the know get on the job, while the lookouts keep guard until the tankers are ready to load.

ANDREA: they've they've worked relatively under the radar for a very long time. criminals work on the basis of what happens in the dark, stays in the dark.

VO: And if it goes according to plan - it’s a good pay day.

INFORMANT: If the pressure is right, maybe it's going to take two hours for the truck, those big trucks, just two hours, and then they bring another strike just two hours // maybe they couldn't ??? wait for the whole night.
MASA: Easy job, big money

ANDREA: this is pure greed because it is clean money in the making. You steal the fuel from the pipeline. There is no middle man. See, it goes straight into a market. // that market doesn't pay the levies that government // So it's a clean profit.

WAAL: it's easy because once you've you've got rid of it and it's in the fuel tank, // it disappears. You can't footprinting. It's gone.

VO: Because it’s difficult to trace, the fuel gets sold quickly on the black market at discounted rates - either going to dodgy depots, petrol stations or large scale consumers of fuel like transporters.

In the last financial year there were 143 theft incidents on the pipeline network. From April this year, there’s been a further 92 hits in just 7 months. More than 16 million litres of fuel has been lost as a result of this crime trend.

SARET: And that's not taking the other expenses and consequences into account.

VO: Saret Knoetze is from Transnet’s Pipeline division.

SARET: Anything that goes wrong with a tampering incident could result in either the death of some community members, fires or contamination.

VO: In December 2019 a tanker caught alight during an attempted theft in Alberton, south of Joburg. These clips are from the scene.

SARET: The threat that it is for the residents living near Pipeline, our pipeline traverses people's backyard close to communities, // due to the theft of the incidents, the risk to the community is increasing

LINK: It might take a couple of days to do the research, a couple of days to do the digging and a couple of hours to steal the diesel, but to fix this will take months, if not years, because of the ecological damage.

KLOPPERS: the thieves are taking more than just the pipeline. You know, they're destroying our natural assets

VO: Conservationist, Dr Roelie Kloppers met us in the Durban Bay area just a week after a crude oil spill into the Umbilo river. This was the result of an attempted theft on a pipeline.

KLOPPERS: if you look here, you'll see how high the oil is, come onto these plants here
MASA: What is the environmental impact of a spill like this?
KLOPPERS: It's all disaster, it's all poison. It doesn't belong in those ecosystems, goes through into those food chains and everything, it feeds all those things

VO: Long term rehabilitation efforts will be necessary to properly restore the area. Knoetze assures us Transnet are onboard.

SARET: Various subject experts on board, aquatic experts, environmental experts that will give us special asplen per zone down the river to address the specific sensitivities of the environment

VO: In JP’s case – the diesel spill on the 2 hectares of farming land will undoubtedly impact on future crops.

JP: talks about the compensation from Transnet has been there. But as far as I'm aware, no compensation has come into our accoutns as of yet.

VO: According to Knoetze, Transnet’s insurance company is dealing with the claim.

While the collateral ecological and economic damage is undeniable, it doesn’t appear to concern the thieves in the slightest.

MASA: we're losing millions and millions of rands?
INFORMANT: Yeah, they know about that. //They don't care about someone else quality in their daily lives and they think about it, their pockets.

VO But they should be thinking about the very real jail sentences they could face if convicted. This is not petty crime - this is essential infrastructure related crime that lends itself to sabotage – explains Advocate Johnson.

If successfully prosecuted in terms of the The Criminal Matters Amendment Act, adopted in 2016, criminals found guilty of tampering, damaging or stealing essential infrastructure can get as much as 30 years direct imprisonment - that is more than murder.

MASA: They seem like quite hefty sentences or do they actually just match the crime
ANDREA: when you look at the ripple effect in terms of the economy// one thinks that if you just steal fifty thousand litres of fuel, it's a drop in the ocean compared to what the country actually requires. But count those drops every day for a month, and we've lost a lot. //. So getting them off the street and giving them that kind of sentence really does match the crime.

VO: The Criminal Matters Ammendment Act also allows for insiders to be dealt with decisively.

ANDREA: Section two allows for charges of collusion by. // we'd be able to apply the Criminal Matters Amendment Act and they face similar sentences as well

VO: The biggest challenge at the moment is catching them in the act.

LINK: With criminals constantly evolving, security companies have to use the latest state of the art technology to stay a step ahead.

WAAL: that's an eye in the sky, pitch darkness, they don't hear, they don't see, // at 50 meters, you won't see all yet. That's the beauty of it. You can watch without being detected and catch them on the act so we can get that information to take to court for successful conviction.

VO: Collaborative investigations run by private security, police and prosecutors are tapping into networks of informants, incorporating suspect profiling and utilising hi-tech surveillance equipment to catch these criminals.

WAAL: technologies are very important to a component to get to that court. // otherwise you catch them and it's a catch and release.

VO To date the joint efforts have secured 110 arrests - with a number of vehicles, tankers and equipment impounded - but more can be done.

ANDREA: As every South African, we should be worried when we are unable to access fuel simply because the fuel is being stolen in the quantities that it's being stolen in.


PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Criminals have a found a way to get their hands onto thousands of litres of free fuel. They’re illegally tapping into an extensive underground network of pipelines. We investigate this new trend.

PROMO 2
VO: Critical Fuel pipelines are being hit by criminal syndicates. It costs the county billions of rands in infrastructure and ecological damage. We investigate this growing crime trend that could cripple the economy.

PROMO 3
VO: Using state of the art technology, air and ground crews The security industry has set its sights on thieves targeting fuel pipelines across South Africa. We investigate this new crime trend.

metadata.Further information: Fuel in South Africa is a top commodity. Hundreds of Millions of litres is transported across the country every week. Criminals are tapping in and feeding a lucrative black market with stolen fuel. The latest crime trend is targeting Transnet’s extensive pipeline network that traverses five province. The modus operandi of the criminals suggest well-organised and equipped gangs are driving the hits. Using engineering equipment, the thieves tap into the pipeline stealing tankers and tankers full of fuel. In the past three months, Transnet had recorded over 200 incidents along its pipeline – pipeline thefts are on the rise. It’s not petty crime – this amounts to essential infrastructure damage and could see very hefty sentences in successful case prosecution. South Africa's infrastructure is being damaged by this theft and vandalism along Transnet’s 3 800km fuel pipeline network. The pipeline network traverses five provinces and transports 250 million liters of petrol and diesel per week. In the past 18 months, Transnet had recorded loses of over 16 million litres to these thefts. The thefts occur in Gauteng and Mpumalanga mainly, however the incidents had become more sporadic along its entire network recently. Transnet said evidence obtained about the modus operandi of the criminals pointed to a well-organised and equipped gang being involved. “Criminals operate in groups, each with a specific task. These criminals are found to be armed, [and they have] no fear for their personal safety.” It’s believed that the criminals approached landowners and promise them financial compensation in exchange for access to land and pipelines. We speak to an affected Farmer, look at the environmental damage, get the inside track from an informant and speak to a security company tackling this crime trend with state of the art technology and old-school intelligence.
